document.title: Memorandum of Conversation: The Secretary's Third Meeting with Shevardnadze, February 21, 1988
document.authors: U.S. Department of State (Dennis Ross Collection, Reagan Library)
document.publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Soviet Withdrawal from Afghanistan 1989 | National Security Archive
document.note: Shultz and Shevardnadze discuss Afghanistan along with the Iran-Iraq war, the Middle East and Central America. The US demands a pledge to cease Soviet military aid to Kabul once an agreement takes effect. Shevardnadze explains the difficulty of abandoning the Kabul government, doubts US willingness to guarantee the accords, and the two end no closer to agreement.

persons.name: George Shultz
persons.role: U.S. Secretary of State leading U.S. delegation in Moscow

mentions.quote: The Secretary expressed the U.S. view that a real opportunity had emerged for a political resolution.
Quoting from the Declaration of Guarantees, THE SECRETARY pointed out that the language on non-interference did not provide for exceptions
THE SECRETARY said that the two ministers' past discussions of Afghanistan had often concluded with the recognition that we saw matters differently.
Shevardnadze could once again assure the Secretary on the instructions of the Soviet leadership that a final decision had been made to withdraw.
Shevardnadze suggested that the Secretary consider how the U.S. would react were Moscow to insist on the termination of U.S. aid to Afghanistan.
SHEVARDNADZE reiterated that it was impossible to start a new process after five years in Geneva, when an agreement was in sight.

events.description: Third meeting between Shultz and Shevardnadze in Moscow; Afghanistan discussed.
Shultz and Shevardnadze met in Washington; Shevardnadze assured Soviet withdrawal decision.
Zia indicated he would sign Geneva accords on this date rather than March 15.
U.S. asked to be guarantor, contingent on satisfactory accord.
Third meeting of Secretary Shultz with Shevardnadze, discussing the Geneva accords, guarantees, aid cutoff, and the Iran-Iraq war.
U.S. asked to act as guarantor, conditional on a satisfactory Geneva accord.
Shultz's third meeting with Shevardnadze on regional issues including Afghanistan.
Shultz–Shevardnadze meeting in Washington where Shevardnadze said the Soviets decided to withdraw from Afghanistan.
Shultz proposed Soviets move out about 20,000 troops in first weeks, frontloading, and cessation of military aid to Kabul upon Geneva agreement.
Shevardnadze assured that a final decision had been made to withdraw Soviet forces from Afghanistan, linked to the next Geneva round.
Planned Soviet goal of complete withdrawal from Afghanistan by end of 1988; planned Reagan visit to Moscow.
Washington summit at which US argued against linking interim government to Soviet withdrawals.
Proposed Geneva signing date that Zia refused, preferring March 30.
Zia's stated date for signing the Geneva accords.
U.S. asked to be guarantor of Geneva accord; agreed contingent on a satisfactory accord.
Shultz and Shevardnadze discuss Afghanistan, guarantor role, interim government and Iran-Iraq war.
Shevardnadze predicted intense Afghanistan discussion in March if no Geneva agreement.
Third Shultz–Shevardnadze meeting discussing Geneva process, withdrawal timetable, refugees, interim government and military aid.
Zia indicated to Vorontsov he would sign the Geneva accords on March 30 rather than March 15.
Date Soviets wanted for signing of Geneva accords, rejected by Zia.
Washington summit where Reagan and Shultz said Afghanistan should be resolved as soon as possible.
Approximately 100,000 refugees reportedly returned home with Soviet help for resettlement.

key_claims: The Soviets stated a final decision had been made to withdraw from Afghanistan, tied to concluding the Geneva talks.
The U.S. sought a front-loaded, short withdrawal timetable with troop movements starting immediately upon entry into force.
The U.S. demanded symmetrical cessation of military aid to Kabul and the resistance, which Shevardnadze resisted.
Shevardnadze said all U.S. aid to the resistance flowed through Pakistan.
Zia's push for an interim government was seen as linked to refugee resettlement and complicated the Geneva process.
Armacost argued Kabul controlled only a small portion of Afghan territory while the resistance controlled much of the country.
The Soviets insisted they could not abandon commitments to Kabul and rejected a symmetrical aid cutoff.
The U.S. said its guarantor role in 1985 was contingent on a satisfactory Geneva accord.
Armacost argued the resistance controlled most Afghan territory while Kabul controlled only a small portion.
Shevardnadze said that after withdrawal Moscow would send food rather than arms to Kabul.
Shevardnadze said Afghanistan's neutrality was for Afghans to decide, not the superpowers.
The Secretary said the U.S. believed the Soviet Union intended to withdraw and wanted to encourage Geneva.
